title: The prayer of the heart
hookLine: bring the mind down into the heart and stand before God

cards: Go down with your mind into your heart, and stand there before God. That's the advice, in substance, of a Russian bishop and hermit the Orthodox church remembers as Saint Theophan the Recluse.
Tradition says he gave it to people who wrote to him asking how to pray. Not louder. Not longer.

Lower. Today, out of the Benedictine cloister and into another room in the house: the Orthodox way of the heart. Tradition counts desert monks and forest hermits among its teachers, and their first lesson is almost a map.
Attention tends to live up in the head, busy and chattering. Bring it down.

teach.b: Start with what the Bible means by heart. It's not only where feelings live. In scripture the heart is the center of a person: where you think, decide, remember, love.

After the shepherds' visit, Luke says, "Mary kept all these things, and pondered them in her heart." Pondering, there, is heart work. And Jesus says, "Blessed are the pure in heart: for they shall see God."
Seeing God, and the heart, in one breath. The Orthodox teachers take that seriously. If the heart is the center, then prayer that stays in the head stays on the surface.
Words said, thoughts thought, while the real you is somewhere else. So they teach a descent.

teach.h: THE MIND COMES DOWN AND SETTLES.
teach.b: The mind, the busy attention, comes down and rests in the heart, the way a bird that's been beating around a room finally settles on a perch. And there, still, you stand before God. Not explaining yourself.
Not performing. Just present. Some who walk this way use a short prayer, said slowly over and over, often in rhythm with the breath.
One form of it runs: Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me. It's called the Jesus Prayer, and it echoes what the blind man and the tax collector say in the Gospels.

Jesus himself gives a picture of the place: "when thou prayest, enter into thy closet, and when thou hast shut thy door, pray to thy Father which is in secret." Some Orthodox teachers hear the closet as the heart. Go in.

how: In Orthodox Christianity, monks, nuns and lay people practice the prayer of the heart, often by repeating the Jesus Prayer slowly, sometimes with a prayer rope, under the guidance of a spiritual father or mother.

games.q: you write to a hermit bishop asking how to pray. your head is full of noise. what does Theophan's advice amount to?
o: go down with your mind into your heart and stand before God.
wait until your head is quiet first.
games.why: Theophan's advice, in substance: bring the mind down into the heart, and stand there before God.

practice: Sit upright, feet on the floor, and notice where your attention is; it may be somewhere behind your eyes.

Let it sink, slowly, to the middle of your chest, and feel your breath there; when a thought pulls you back up, notice, and let it sink again. If you pray, say the Jesus Prayer quietly with the breath; if not, just rest there.
